sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This document describes the reference data set RDS-CRR-2025.1 used to develop, calibrate and validate version 4.0 of model MDL-16 AML Customer Risk Rating (CRR), and it follows the RDS documentation template of Annex A to MRM-STD-021. MDL-16 assigns every customer of the Bank a risk class (Low, Medium, High or Unacceptable) that determines the intensity of customer due diligence; it is a weighted risk-factor scoring model with fixed expert-based weights over five domains (customer, geography, products and services, delivery channel and behaviour), supplemented by mandatory high-risk triggers, and it is registered in the Model Inventory as a Tier 2 FEC model. Although the CRR involves no statistical estimation, it is treated as a model under MRM-POL-001 and FEC-STD-600 §2.2 and is managed across the full model lifecycle. The scope of application comprises all customers of the Bank in the Netherlands: retail natural persons, sole proprietors, small and medium-sized enterprises, corporates and financial institutions and other legal entities, with the exception of correspondent banking relationships, which are rated under the correspondent due diligence methodology of Financial Crime Compliance. The companion documents are the CRR methodology document EVD-16-MDD, the expert panel minutes EVD-16-EXP, the implementation and testing report EVD-16-IMPL and the annual monitoring and back-testing report EVD-16-MON.

sections.heading: Observation period
sections.text: The RDS consists of two annual customer cohorts: cohort 2023 with risk-factor values as at 31 March 2023 and outcomes observed from 1 April 2023 to 31 March 2024, and cohort 2024 with risk-factor values as at 31 March 2024 and outcomes from 1 April 2024 to 31 March 2025; the snapshot frequency is annual and outcomes are recorded monthly. After exclusions cohort 2023 contains 2,729,250 customers with 7,560 customers with an adverse outcome (0.28%) and cohort 2024 contains 2,768,900 customers with 8,290 adverse outcomes (0.30%); in total the RDS contains 2,812,640 unique customers. An adverse outcome is any of the three target events defined in section 3.1: an unusual transaction report (MOT) filed on the customer, an exit of the relationship for integrity reasons, or a transaction of the customer declared suspicious by FIU-Nederland. In cohort 2023 there were 6,480 customers with an MOT, 1,690 integrity exits and 1,040 FIU declarations; in cohort 2024 7,150, 1,820 and 1,130 respectively.

sections.heading: Choice of observation window
sections.text: The window starts in March 2023 because the CDD questionnaire of KYC-One was redesigned in January 2023, introducing the expected-activity fields (expected turnover, cash use and countries) that feed several risk factors; earlier snapshots lack these fields for most customers. The cohort 2023 serves as development sample, randomly split 70/30 by customer into development and out-of-sample parts for the statistical benchmark, and the cohort 2024 serves as out-of-time sample; both samples were defined on 14 March 2025 before any factor analysis. Two cohorts cover the introduction of instant payments at scale, the post-2022 sanctions environment and the growth of money-mule activity, which are the most relevant changes in the Bank's risk environment according to the SIRA 2024 and SIRA 2025.

sections.heading: Target variable
sections.text: MDL-16 does not use a default-based target. In accordance with Annex A of MRM-STD-021, chapter 3 documents the target variable in section 3.1, and sections 3.3 and 3.4 are retained with the statement Not applicable. The CRR is an expert model: the target events are not used to estimate the weights but to test the relevance of risk factors, to benchmark the expert weights against a statistical alternative and to back-test the resulting classes.

sections.heading: Target variable and outcome horizon
sections.text: The target is a composite adverse outcome within twelve months after the snapshot date: an MOT filed on the customer, an exit for integrity reasons decided by the Customer Integrity Committee, or a transaction of the customer declared suspicious by FIU-Nederland, taken from the case management system FCM-CM and the exit register. The twelve-month horizon matches the annual back-testing of FEC-STD-600 §9.4 and the annual review cycle of High-risk customers. Each constituent is also analysed separately, because MOTs are the most frequent but least specific event and FIU declarations the least frequent but most specific. The risk-factor values are taken as at the snapshot date only; information that arises after the snapshot, including alerts and reports that are part of the outcome, is not used as a factor value for the same cohort.

sections.heading: Default definition and unlikeliness-to-pay triggers
sections.text: Not applicable: the model does not estimate default probabilities and does not use days-past-due counting, materiality thresholds, probation periods, unlikeliness-to-pay triggers or historical approximations of a default flag. Customers with more than one adverse event in the outcome window are counted once in the composite outcome and once per event type in the separate analyses.

sections.heading: Data sources and lineage
sections.text: The RDS is sourced from eight source systems mapped to five data domains in the Group Data Catalogue: Customer (KYC-One CDD questionnaires, Customer Master Data), Products (product administration of the core banking platform), Channels (digital onboarding logs), FEC Case (FCM-CM alerts, MOTs and FIU feedback; exit register) and External Data (Chamber of Commerce trade and UBO register, PEP and adverse media data from an external provider, EU list of high-risk third countries). Each domain has exactly one Data Owner recorded in the Group Data Catalogue: the Head of Client Data Management (Customer), the Head of Retail Products (Products), the Head of Digital Channels (Channels), the Head of Transaction Monitoring Operations (FEC Case) and the Chief Data Officer's external data office (External Data). Data are extracted into the FEC Data Hub (FDH) by the dbt project fdh-crr (jobs fdh_crr_customer, fdh_crr_products, fdh_crr_fec and fdh_crr_external) and transformed into factor values by the build code in repository fec-analytics/crr-rds; Annex A documents for every one of the 64 variables, including the 21 discarded variables used to construct retained factors, the source system and field, each intermediate store, every transformation, filter, join and aggregation with a reference to the dbt model or Python function, and the extraction frequency and timing. Factors are computed at customer level across all products and accounts of the business relationship, so that the rating covers every product and service the customer holds.

sections.heading: Exclusions
sections.text: Three exclusions were applied per cohort, each quantified by the build code: (a) 1,260 internal and staff test customers (0.05%); (b) 9,870 customers in estate settlement after death (0.36%), because the relationship is in wind-down and no longer rated; (c) 6,420 customers of the discontinued Belgian branch (0.23%, cohort 2023 only), which are outside the current range of application. The impact analysis in section 5.3 concludes that none of the exclusions affects the representativeness of the RDS for the current portfolio; no exclusion exceeds 5% of the records of any segment. Customers with incomplete CDD data from the legacy onboarding period before 2019 are not excluded; they are retained with missing-value indicators (section 4.3), because excluding them would remove a population with an above-average adverse-outcome rate.

sections.heading: Missing values and outliers
sections.text: Missing values are documented per variable in Annex C and classified as structural (for example no UBO data for natural persons), missing at random (0.3% of onboarding channel codes) or missing because of a data deficiency (expected activity missing for 6.8% of sole proprietors onboarded before 2019, DD-CRR-01). Where a factor value is missing because of a data deficiency, the factor receives the highest score of its scale (5) until the CDD data are completed, a conservative and reproducible rule implemented in the build code; 1.9% of customers carry at least one such default score, and the effect is an increase of the High share by 0.2 percentage points. Outliers in the continuous inputs of the behaviour domain (turnover deviation ratio and cash intensity) are identified by the documented rule of values above the 99.9th percentile per segment and capped at that percentile identically in development and production; the caps affect 0.1% of values and change the class of fewer than 0.01% of customers. The target events are never imputed: 212 outcome records with an inconsistent customer link were corrected at source in FCM-CM under ticket FEC-DQ-2025-031 before the RDS was frozen.

sections.heading: Representativeness
sections.text: Representativeness was tested against the customer population as at 31 December 2024: the PSI of the CRR score between cohort 2023 and the reference population is 0.04, the PSI of the individual factors ranges from 0.00 to 0.08, and the shares of segments differ by less than one percentage point. The adverse-outcome rate of cohort 2024 (0.30%) is higher than that of cohort 2023 (0.28%), a difference that is significant at 5% but small in relative terms (7%), and it is explained by the growth of MOTs on money-mule accounts, which is represented in the behaviour domain. The financial institutions and other legal entities segment (3,720 customers in cohort 2024) is small and has a volatile outcome rate; this is recorded as limitation L-CRR-03 in the MDD.

sections.heading: Representativeness for other uses
sections.text: The CRR class is also used as an input by the transaction monitoring model MDL-15 (thresholds and prioritisation feature). This use relies on the same customer population and requires no separate representativeness analysis; the effect of CRR changes on MDL-15 is assessed under the change notification described in the MDD. The CRR is not used outside the population of the RDS, for example for correspondent banks or for prospective customers who do not complete onboarding.

sections.heading: Impact of exclusions
sections.text: Exclusion (a) removes records without economic content. Exclusion (b) removes customers with a low outcome rate (0.05%) whose inclusion would slightly understate the outcome rate of retail Low-class customers. Exclusion (c) removes customers of a branch that no longer exists; their adverse-outcome rate (0.61%) was above average and not representative of the current portfolio. Recomputing the factor distributions and the outcome rates per class with all exclusions reversed changes no factor PSI by more than 0.01 and no class outcome rate by more than 0.02 percentage points.

sections.heading: Data quality assessment
sections.text: The data quality of the RDS was assessed before development on 22 April 2025 on completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, validity and uniqueness for all 43 critical data elements, which comprise every retained factor input and the constituents of the adverse outcome. Completeness was measured at record level (all active customers of Customer Master Data present in each cohort) and at attribute level (at least 99% non-missing for 38 of 43 elements; expected activity fields between 93.2% and 97.4%). Accuracy was measured by reconciling customer counts per segment with Customer Master Data and product counts with the product administration, and by a sample of 300 customer files checked against the source documents in KYC-One, in which 296 files matched on all checked fields. Consistency was tested between the RDS and the production CRR input tables on the same reference date and through 27 logical rules (for example legal form consistent with segment and UBO data present for all legal entities), and timeliness as the currency of the CDD review date against the review frequency of the customer's class. The assessment reports the result of each rule per variable and dimension against its thresholds and the number and share of excluded records per exclusion reason, concludes that the RDS is fit for the development of CRR version 4.0, and was signed off by the lead developer and the model owner on 25 April 2025 before the RDS was frozen.

sections.heading: Data quality rules and thresholds
sections.text: For every critical data element at least one rule is defined for each applicable mandatory dimension, and the reason is recorded where a dimension is not applicable, for example timeliness for the static legal form. The rules are documented in Annex C and implemented as recurring checks in the Group DQ monitoring tool, rule set DQ-FEC-CRR-v4 (141 rules), which is also applied to the daily production input data of the CRR engine. Each rule has an amber and a red threshold at least as strict as the MRM-STD-022 defaults (completeness amber below 98% and red below 95%, accuracy amber above 0.5% and red above 1%, consistency amber below 99% and red below 98%), and the outcome constituents (MOT reference, exit reason, FIU declaration) have a completeness red threshold of 99.5%. The temporary deviation for the expected activity fields of sole proprietors (amber below 90%) is justified in Annex C by the CDD remediation programme and was approved by the model owner on 15 April 2025.

sections.heading: Currency of customer due diligence data
sections.text: The currency of customer information is monitored against the review frequencies of FEC-POL-001 §5.5: at the snapshot of 31 March 2024, 98.2% of High-risk customers had been reviewed within the last twelve months and 96.9% of Medium-risk and 97.5% of Low-risk customers within three and five years respectively. Customer data are also updated when relevant circumstances change: changes reported through the Chamber of Commerce mutation service, returned mail, screening hits and productive TM alerts trigger an event-driven review, and 94.8% of those reviews were completed within 30 days. The data feeds used for the CRR are reconciled monthly with the source systems, and data gaps are reported to Financial Crime Compliance.

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This document describes the reference data set RDS-CRR-2025.1 used to develop, calibrate and validate version 4.0 of model MDL-16 AML Customer Risk Rating (CRR), and it follows the RDS documentation template of Annex A to MRM-STD-021. MDL-16 assigns every customer of the Bank a risk class (Low, Medium, High or Unacceptable) that determines the intensity of customer due diligence; it is a weighted risk-factor scoring model with fixed expert-based weights over five domains (customer, geography, products and services, delivery channel and behaviour), supplemented by mandatory high-risk triggers, and it is registered in the Model Inventory as a Tier 2 FEC model. Although the CRR involves no statistical estimation, it is treated as a model under MRM-POL-001 and FEC-STD-600 §2.2 and is managed across the full model lifecycle. The scope of application comprises all customers of the Bank in the Netherlands: retail natural persons, sole proprietors, small and medium-sized enterprises, corporates and financial institutions and other legal entities, with the exception of correspondent banking relationships, which are rated under the correspondent due diligence methodology of Financial Crime Compliance. The companion documents are the CRR methodology document EVD-16-MDD, the expert panel minutes EVD-16-EXP, the implementation and testing report EVD-16-IMPL and the annual monitoring and back-testing report EVD-16-MON.

sections.heading: Observation period
sections.text: The RDS consists of two annual customer cohorts: cohort 2023 with risk-factor values as at 31 March 2023 and outcomes observed from 1 April 2023 to 31 March 2024, and cohort 2024 with risk-factor values as at 31 March 2024 and outcomes from 1 April 2024 to 31 March 2025; the snapshot frequency is annual and outcomes are recorded monthly. After exclusions cohort 2023 contains 2,729,250 customers with 7,560 customers with an adverse outcome (0.28%) and cohort 2024 contains 2,768,900 customers with 8,290 adverse outcomes (0.30%); in total the RDS contains 2,812,640 unique customers. An adverse outcome is any of the three target events defined in section 3.1: an unusual transaction report (MOT) filed on the customer, an exit of the relationship for integrity reasons, or a transaction of the customer declared suspicious by FIU-Nederland. In cohort 2023 there were 6,480 customers with an MOT, 1,690 integrity exits and 1,040 FIU declarations; in cohort 2024 7,150, 1,820 and 1,130 respectively.

sections.heading: Choice of observation window
sections.text: The window starts in March 2023 because the CDD questionnaire of KYC-One was redesigned in January 2023, introducing the expected-activity fields (expected turnover, cash use and countries) that feed several risk factors; earlier snapshots lack these fields for most customers. The cohort 2023 serves as development sample, randomly split 70/30 by customer into development and out-of-sample parts for the statistical benchmark, and the cohort 2024 serves as out-of-time sample; both samples were defined on 14 March 2025 before any factor analysis. Two cohorts cover the introduction of instant payments at scale, the post-2022 sanctions environment and the growth of money-mule activity, which are the most relevant changes in the Bank's risk environment according to the SIRA 2024 and SIRA 2025.

sections.heading: Target variable
sections.text: MDL-16 does not use a default-based target. In accordance with Annex A of MRM-STD-021, chapter 3 documents the target variable in section 3.1, and sections 3.3 and 3.4 are retained with the statement Not applicable. The CRR is an expert model: the target events are not used to estimate the weights but to test the relevance of risk factors, to benchmark the expert weights against a statistical alternative and to back-test the resulting classes.

sections.heading: Target variable and outcome horizon
sections.text: The target is a composite adverse outcome within twelve months after the snapshot date: an MOT filed on the customer, an exit for integrity reasons decided by the Customer Integrity Committee, or a transaction of the customer declared suspicious by FIU-Nederland, taken from the case management system FCM-CM and the exit register. The twelve-month horizon matches the annual back-testing of FEC-STD-600 §9.4 and the annual review cycle of High-risk customers. Each constituent is also analysed separately, because MOTs are the most frequent but least specific event and FIU declarations the least frequent but most specific. The risk-factor values are taken as at the snapshot date only; information that arises after the snapshot, including alerts and reports that are part of the outcome, is not used as a factor value for the same cohort.

sections.heading: Data sources and lineage

Each domain has exactly one Data Owner recorded in the Group Data Catalogue: the Head of Client Data Management (Customer), the Head of Retail Products (Products), the Head of Digital Channels (Channels), the Head of Transaction Monitoring Operations (FEC Case) and the Chief Data Officer's external data office (External Data). Data are extracted into the FEC Data Hub (FDH) by the dbt project fdh-crr (jobs fdh_crr_customer, fdh_crr_products, fdh_crr_fec and fdh_crr_external) and transformed into factor values by the build code in repository fec-analytics/crr-rds; Annex A documents for every one of the 64 variables, including the 21 discarded variables used to construct retained factors, the source system and field, each intermediate store, every transformation, filter, join and aggregation with a reference to the dbt model or Python function, and the extraction frequency and timing. Factors are computed at customer level across all products and accounts of the business relationship, so that the rating covers every product and service the customer holds.

sections.heading: Exclusions
sections.text: Three exclusions were applied per cohort, each quantified by the build code: (a) 1,260 internal and staff test customers (0.05%); (b) 9,870 customers in estate settlement after death (0.36%), because the relationship is in wind-down and no longer rated; (c) 6,420 customers of the discontinued Belgian branch (0.23%, cohort 2023 only), which are outside the current range of application. The impact analysis in section 5.3 concludes that none of the exclusions affects the representativeness of the RDS for the current portfolio; no exclusion exceeds 5% of the records of any segment. Customers with incomplete CDD data from the legacy onboarding period before 2019 are not excluded; they are retained with missing-value indicators (section 4.3), because excluding them would remove a population with an above-average adverse-outcome rate.

sections.heading: Missing values and outliers
sections.text: Missing values are documented per variable in Annex C and classified as structural (for example no UBO data for natural persons), missing at random (0.3% of onboarding channel codes) or missing because of a data deficiency (expected activity missing for 6.8% of sole proprietors onboarded before 2019, DD-CRR-01). Where a factor value is missing because of a data deficiency, the factor receives the highest score of its scale (5) until the CDD data are completed, a conservative and reproducible rule implemented in the build code; 1.9% of customers carry at least one such default score, and the effect is an increase of the High share by 0.2 percentage points. Outliers in the continuous inputs of the behaviour domain (turnover deviation ratio and cash intensity) are identified by the documented rule of values above the 99.9th percentile per segment and capped at that percentile identically in development and production; the caps affect 0.1% of values and change the class of fewer than 0.01% of customers. The target events are never imputed: 212 outcome records with an inconsistent customer link were corrected at source in FCM-CM under ticket FEC-DQ-2025-031 before the RDS was frozen.

sections.heading: Representativeness
sections.text: Representativeness was tested against the customer population as at 31 December 2024: the PSI of the CRR score between cohort 2023 and the reference population is 0.04, the PSI of the individual factors ranges from 0.00 to 0.08, and the shares of segments differ by less than one percentage point. The adverse-outcome rate of cohort 2024 (0.30%) is higher than that of cohort 2023 (0.28%), a difference that is significant at 5% but small in relative terms (7%), and it is explained by the growth of MOTs on money-mule accounts, which is represented in the behaviour domain. The financial institutions and other legal entities segment (3,720 customers in cohort 2024) is small and has a volatile outcome rate; this is recorded as limitation L-CRR-03 in the MDD.

sections.heading: Representativeness for other uses
sections.text: The CRR class is also used as an input by the transaction monitoring model MDL-15 (thresholds and prioritisation feature). This use relies on the same customer population and requires no separate representativeness analysis; the effect of CRR changes on MDL-15 is assessed under the change notification described in the MDD. The CRR is not used outside the population of the RDS, for example for correspondent banks or for prospective customers who do not complete onboarding.

sections.heading: Impact of exclusions
sections.text: Exclusion (a) removes records without economic content. Exclusion (b) removes customers with a low outcome rate (0.05%) whose inclusion would slightly understate the outcome rate of retail Low-class customers. Exclusion (c) removes customers of a branch that no longer exists; their adverse-outcome rate (0.61%) was above average and not representative of the current portfolio. Recomputing the factor distributions and the outcome rates per class with all exclusions reversed changes no factor PSI by more than 0.01 and no class outcome rate by more than 0.02 percentage points.

sections.heading: Data quality assessment
sections.text: The data quality of the RDS was assessed before development on 22 April 2025 on completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, validity and uniqueness for all 43 critical data elements, which comprise every retained factor input and the constituents of the adverse outcome. Completeness was measured at record level (all active customers of Customer Master Data present in each cohort) and at attribute level (at least 99% non-missing for 38 of 43 elements; expected activity fields between 93.2% and 97.4%). Accuracy was measured by reconciling customer counts per segment with Customer Master Data and product counts with the product administration, and by a sample of 300 customer files checked against the source documents in KYC-One, in which 296 files matched on all checked fields. Consistency was tested between the RDS and the production CRR input tables on the same reference date and through 27 logical rules (for example legal form consistent with segment and UBO data present for all legal entities), and timeliness as the currency of the CDD review date against the review frequency of the customer's class. The assessment reports the result of each rule per variable and dimension against its thresholds and the number and share of excluded records per exclusion reason, concludes that the RDS is fit for the development of CRR version 4.0, and was signed off by the lead developer and the model owner on 25 April 2025 before the RDS was frozen.

The temporary deviation for the expected activity fields of sole proprietors (amber below 90%) is justified in Annex C by the CDD remediation programme and was approved by the model owner on 15 April 2025.

sections.heading: Currency of customer due diligence data
sections.text: The currency of customer information is monitored against the review frequencies of FEC-POL-001 §5.5: at the snapshot of 31 March 2024, 98.2% of High-risk customers had been reviewed within the last twelve months and 96.9% of Medium-risk and 97.5% of Low-risk customers within three and five years respectively. Customer data are also updated when relevant circumstances change: changes reported through the Chamber of Commerce mutation service, returned mail, screening hits and productive TM alerts trigger an event-driven review, and 94.8% of those reviews were completed within 30 days. The data feeds used for the CRR are reconciled monthly with the source systems, and data gaps are reported to Financial Crime Compliance.

sections.heading: Personal data attributes and minimisation
sections.text: The RDS contains 26 personal data attributes, each justified in Annex A by its relevance to the risk classification, together with its lawful basis, the pseudonymisation applied and the retention period; names, addresses, dates of birth and free-text CDD answers are not included. Only data obtained under customer due diligence, the Bank's own transaction and case data and public register data are used; no social media or data broker information is processed. No special categories of personal data under Art. 9(1) GDPR are processed: nationality, which is not a special category but can act as a proxy for ethnic origin, was removed as a factor in version 4.0 and replaced by the country of residence and transactional geography. By default each processing step receives only the attributes it needs: the factor pipeline outputs factor scores, and the development environment has no access to identifiers or free-text fields.

sections.heading: Purpose, scope and intended use
sections.text: This methodology document (MDD) documents version 4.0 of MDL-16 AML Customer Risk Rating and follows the chapter structure, numbering and headings of the MDD template in Annex B to MRM-STD-021. sections.heading: Regulatory context
sections.text: The CRR implements the risk-based approach of Articles 2b, 3(7) and 8 of the Wwft and chapter 3 of the DNB Guidance on the Wwft and the Sanctions Act, and it prepares the Bank for Articles 20, 26 and 34 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 (AMLR), which applies from 10 July 2027. The Bank classifies its entire customer base into risk categories based on objective, identifiable factors that cover all risk factors that could affect the integrity risk of the relationship, and the classification system is documented in writing in this MDD and summarised in the Customer Acceptance Policy FCC-POL-004. Four classes are used, consistent with the nature, size and complexity of the Bank's risk factors: Low, Medium and High determine the intensity of CDD, and Unacceptable means that the relationship is not entered into or is terminated. The CRR supports the Bank in demonstrating to DNB that the CDD measures taken are appropriate in view of the identified risks, because every class assignment is stored with its factor scores, triggers and CDD measures.

sections.heading: Model design
sections.text: The CRR score is the weighted sum of five domain scores on a scale from 1 (lowest risk) to 5 (highest risk): customer characteristics (weight 30%), geography (25%), products and services (20%), delivery channel (10%) and behaviour (15%); each domain score is the weighted average of the scores of its factors, and the resulting score is mapped to the classes Low (below 2.20), Medium (2.20 to below 3.20) and High (3.20 or higher). Mandatory triggers (section 5.3) override the calculated score and assign at least High, and Unacceptable criteria assign the class Unacceptable irrespective of the score. The score is recalculated nightly for all customers in the CRR engine whenever a factor value changes. In addition to the class, the CRR produces an individual risk profile consisting of the domain scores, the three factors with the highest contribution and the active triggers, which is shown to CDD analysts and used by transaction monitoring.

sections.heading: Periodic and event-driven reviews
sections.text: The frequency of periodic customer file reviews is determined by the class: at least annually for High, every three years for Medium and every five years for Low, which is within the maximum intervals of one year for customers under enhanced due diligence and five years for other customers. Event-driven reviews are triggered by productive transaction monitoring alerts and MOTs, sanctions, PEP and adverse media screening hits, changes in beneficial ownership, legal form or registered address from the Chamber of Commerce mutation service, a move to a high-risk jurisdiction, requests from FIU-Nederland or law enforcement, returned mail and the take-up of a product in the highest product risk class. The effectiveness of the event-driven triggers is demonstrated in the monitoring report: in 2024, 58,300 event-driven reviews under version 3.2 led to a class increase in 8.1% of cases, compared with 2.0% for periodic reviews. Every review records the CDD actions taken, the decisions with their justification and the supporting documents in KYC-One, and the record is updated at each review.

sections.heading: Dependencies on other models and systems
sections.text: The CRR uses outputs of the transaction monitoring model MDL-15 (productive alerts and MOTs in the behaviour domain) and of the sanctions and PEP screening platform (triggers). MDL-15 in turn uses the CRR class for its thresholds and prioritisation. To avoid circular amplification, the CRR uses only analyst-confirmed outcomes (productive alerts and MOTs), not MDL-15 priority scores. Changes to MDL-16 are notified to the MDL-15 model owner before implementation, and the effect on MDL-15 alert volumes is estimated in the change memorandum; for version 4.0 the estimated increase of MDL-15 alerts was 1.2%.

sections.heading: Alternatives considered
sections.text: Two alternative methodologies were assessed against documented criteria (regulatory expectations, data, performance, stability, interpretability and implementation): (1) the expert weighted scoring of version 3.2 extended with a behaviour domain and (2) a logistic regression of the adverse outcome on the factor scores. The expert weighted scoring was selected because it covers legislative risk factors that have few adverse outcomes in the data (for example correspondent-like services and trust-like arrangements), because it is transparent to CDD analysts and customers, and because the regression would give the behaviour domain a weight of 24% that is partly driven by the overlap between behaviour factors and the outcome; the regression is retained as benchmark (section 7.3). A machine-learning approach was not considered because the purpose of the CRR, a documented and explainable classification based on legislative risk factors, does not require it and because it would bring the model within the scope of AI-POL-001.

sections.heading: Risk factor selection
sections.text: Of 43 candidate factors derived from the SIRA and the legislative risk factors, each was assessed for economic rationale, availability at onboarding and during the relationship, and stability over the two cohorts; 18 factors were retained, and the rejected factors are listed with the reason in annex MDD-B. The selection used univariate analysis of the adverse-outcome rate per factor score, correlation analysis between factors (factors with Spearman correlation above 0.7 were merged, for example cash use declared and cash intensity observed) and the multivariate benchmark regression; every retained factor has a sign consistent with its risk rationale, and none has a negative contribution in the benchmark. Nationality was removed as a factor because it does not add discriminatory power once country of residence and transactional geography are included (benchmark AUC change below 0.001) and because it may act as a proxy for ethnic origin; the Bank does not take decisions that would lead to biased or discriminatory outcomes on the basis of such characteristics.

sections.heading: Domain and factor weights
sections.text: The domain weights of 30% (customer), 25% (geography), 20% (products and services), 10% (delivery channel) and 15% (behaviour) were set by the expert panel of May and June 2025 with a two-round Delphi procedure, documented in EVD-16-EXP, using the SIRA 2025 and the statistical benchmark as inputs. Within the domains the factor weights are: customer – legal form 30%, industry or occupation 35%, ownership complexity 20%, relationship age 15%; geography – country of residence or incorporation 45%, countries of beneficial owners and representatives 25%, expected transaction countries 30%; products – product risk class 60%, declared cash use 20%, international payments 20%; channel – onboarding channel 70%, third-party payment initiation 30%; behaviour – productive TM alerts in 12 months 40%, MOTs in 24 months 35%, turnover deviation from expected activity 25%. The panel weighted behaviour lower than the benchmark (15% instead of 24%) because behaviour factors partly anticipate the outcome events and would otherwise make the class self-reinforcing; this judgement is recorded as EJ-CRR-01.

sections.heading: Factor scoring
sections.text: Each factor is scored from 1 to 5 using scoring tables approved by Financial Crime Compliance. Examples: country of residence scores 1 for EU/EEA countries of Country Risk Matrix class 1, 3 for class 3 and 5 for class 5; industry scores follow the industry risk list with 5 for cash-intensive and high-value-goods sectors such as car dealers and money service businesses; ownership complexity scores 5 for three or more ownership layers or nominee structures; the onboarding channel scores 1 for face-to-face, 2 for video identification and 3 for fully remote app onboarding. Behaviour factors score 1 when no productive alert or MOT exists and rise to 5 for two or more productive alerts in twelve months or an MOT in 24 months; the turnover deviation factor scores 5 when the observed twelve-month turnover exceeds three times the expected activity. The complete scoring tables with the rationale for each score are given in annex MDD-B and are stored in the versioned parameter file crr_scoring_v4.0.csv.

sections.heading: Mandatory triggers and Unacceptable criteria

sections.heading: Material assumptions
sections.text: The material assumptions were identified and assessed for plausibility: (A1) the composite adverse outcome is a reasonable indicator of integrity risk, although it reflects only detected cases; (A2) the legislative risk factors are relevant even where few outcomes are observed; (A3) CDD information is sufficiently current, supported by the review timeliness of 97% or more per class; and (A4) the relationship between factors and outcomes is stable over at least one year, supported by the out-of-time results. Assumption A1 implies that the back-testing cannot measure undetected risk; the model therefore relies on the expert assessment of legislative risk factors in addition to outcome data.

sections.heading: Monitoring plan and KPIs
sections.text: The monitoring plan, approved by the model owner on 10 February 2026 before go-live and reviewed by Model Validation – Financial Crime, defines for each KPI its calculation, amber and red thresholds, frequency, data and reference period, segments, responsible person and escalation, and it is reviewed at least annually and whenever the model changes. The KPIs are: (a) AUC of the score for the composite adverse outcome (amber below 0.72, red below 0.70); (b) monotonic incidence per outcome and class; (c) PSI of the score and of each factor against the development cohort (amber 0.10–0.25, red above 0.25); (d) High share against the SIRA expectation (amber outside 3%–5%, red outside 2%–6%); (e) share of customers with a missing or outdated class (amber above 0.5%, red above 1%); (f) override rates by segment and direction; (g) timeliness of periodic reviews per class. KPIs are computed for the whole model and for each segment and class, and override rates are assessed against the thresholds of MRM-STD-023 §6.2 and the 5% segment trigger of FEC-STD-600 §9.5. A red outcome triggers a review by the model owner and notification of Model Risk Management and Model Validation.

sections.heading: Frequency, reporting and escalation
sections.text: As a Tier 2 model MDL-16 is monitored semi-annually, with the annual report including the back-testing of FEC-STD-600 §9.4, and results are reported within 60 calendar days after the end of the reference period. Each amber result is analysed by the model owner and its cause documented; a red result, or amber on the same KPI in two consecutive cycles, is notified to Model Risk Management and Model Validation within ten business days, followed within 60 calendar days by a root cause analysis and an action plan proposing no action with justification, an overlay, recalibration, redevelopment or restriction of use. The monitoring report shows each KPI with value, threshold, traffic light and trend over the last four cycles, and presents overrides by direction, reason, magnitude and approving unit with the subsequent adverse-outcome rate of overridden and non-overridden customers. Monitoring code (repository fec-analytics/crr-monitoring) and data snapshots are version controlled so that the results are reproducible.

sections.heading: Materiality, challenge and approval
sections.text: Each judgement was classified as low, medium or high materiality against the MRM-STD-023 thresholds, measured as the share of customers changing class compared with the best statistical alternative (the benchmark weights); EJ-CRR-01 and EJ-CRR-03 change the class of more than 10% of customers and are high. Low judgements were approved by the model owner, medium judgements by the model owner and the Head of FEC Analytics Modelling, and the high judgements EJ-CRR-01 and EJ-CRR-03 by the Model Risk Committee on 16 October 2025 after review by Model Validation; no proposer was the sole approver. All medium and high judgements were challenged by Financial Crime Compliance, independent of the CRR Modelling team, and the challenge and its resolution are recorded in the log; the aggregate effect of all judgements compared with the benchmark is a class change for 12.4% of customers, which was approved by the Model Risk Committee. The judgements are reviewed at every annual model review and when new data could replace them.

sections.text: Overrides are permitted only under the CRR override procedure CDD-PRC-012, which specifies the permitted reasons (information not captured by the factors, such as source of wealth evidence or adverse information below the trigger level), the maximum change of one class downwards (no limit upwards), the required evidence and the approval authority (senior CDD officer; Financial Crime Compliance for downward overrides of High). Each override records the reason code, the supporting evidence and the approver in KYC-One. No overlays are applied to the CRR.

sections.heading: Purpose, scope and intended use
sections.text: This methodology document (MDD) documents version 4.0 of MDL-16 AML Customer Risk Rating and follows the chapter structure, numbering and headings of the MDD template in Annex B to MRM-STD-021; chapter 6 is retained with the statement Not applicable. Cover block: title CRR methodology document; model identifier MDL-16; model version 4.0; document version 1.1; status Approved; author E. van Dijk (lead developer); reviewer T. Brouwer (senior developer, review of version 1.1 completed 17 February 2026); approvers M. Bakker (model owner) and P. de Graaf (Head of FEC Analytics Modelling); approval date 20 February 2026. The purpose of MDL-16 is to assign every customer a Customer Risk Rating (Low, Medium, High or Unacceptable) at onboarding and throughout the relationship, using the approved CRR methodology, so that the extent of customer due diligence is determined by an individual analysis of the money-laundering and terrorist-financing risk of the customer. The class determines the CDD measures (simplified, standard or enhanced), the frequency of periodic reviews, the thresholds of transaction monitoring (MDL-15) and the approval level for entering or continuing the relationship; secondary uses are management information for the SIRA and the prioritisation feature of MDL-15.

sections.heading: Model design
sections.text: The CRR score is the weighted sum of five domain scores on a scale from 1 (lowest risk) to 5 (highest risk): customer characteristics (weight 30%), geography (25%), products and services (20%), delivery channel (10%) and behaviour (15%); each domain score is the weighted average of the scores of its factors, and the resulting score is mapped to the classes Low (below 2.20), Medium (2.20 to below 3.20) and High (3.20 or higher). Mandatory triggers (section 5.3) override the calculated score and assign at least High, and Unacceptable criteria assign the class Unacceptable irrespective of the score. The score is recalculated nightly for all customers in the CRR engine whenever a factor value changes. In addition to the class, the CRR produces an individual risk profile consisting of the domain scores, the three factors with the highest contribution and the active triggers, which is shown to CDD analysts and used by transaction monitoring.

sections.heading: Periodic and event-driven reviews
sections.text: The frequency of periodic customer file reviews is determined by the class: at least annually for High, every three years for Medium and every five years for Low, which is within the maximum intervals of one year for customers under enhanced due diligence and five years for other customers. Event-driven reviews are triggered by productive transaction monitoring alerts and MOTs, sanctions, PEP and adverse media screening hits, changes in beneficial ownership, legal form or registered address from the Chamber of Commerce mutation service, a move to a high-risk jurisdiction, requests from FIU-Nederland or law enforcement, returned mail and the take-up of a product in the highest product risk class. The effectiveness of the event-driven triggers is demonstrated in the monitoring report: in 2024, 58,300 event-driven reviews under version 3.2 led to a class increase in 8.1% of cases, compared with 2.0% for periodic reviews. Every review records the CDD actions taken, the decisions with their justification and the supporting documents in KYC-One, and the record is updated at each review.

sections.text: The CRR uses outputs of the transaction monitoring model MDL-15 (productive alerts and MOTs in the behaviour domain) and of the sanctions and PEP screening platform (triggers). sections.heading: Alternatives considered
sections.text: Two alternative methodologies were assessed against documented criteria (regulatory expectations, data, performance, stability, interpretability and implementation): (1) the expert weighted scoring of version 3.2 extended with a behaviour domain and (2) a logistic regression of the adverse outcome on the factor scores. The expert weighted scoring was selected because it covers legislative risk factors that have few adverse outcomes in the data (for example correspondent-like services and trust-like arrangements), because it is transparent to CDD analysts and customers, and because the regression would give the behaviour domain a weight of 24% that is partly driven by the overlap between behaviour factors and the outcome; the regression is retained as benchmark (section 7.3). A machine-learning approach was not considered because the purpose of the CRR, a documented and explainable classification based on legislative risk factors, does not require it and because it would bring the model within the scope of AI-POL-001.

sections.heading: Risk factor selection
sections.text: Of 43 candidate factors derived from the SIRA and the legislative risk factors, each was assessed for economic rationale, availability at onboarding and during the relationship, and stability over the two cohorts; 18 factors were retained, and the rejected factors are listed with the reason in annex MDD-B. The selection used univariate analysis of the adverse-outcome rate per factor score, correlation analysis between factors (factors with Spearman correlation above 0.7 were merged, for example cash use declared and cash intensity observed) and the multivariate benchmark regression; every retained factor has a sign consistent with its risk rationale, and none has a negative contribution in the benchmark. Nationality was removed as a factor because it does not add discriminatory power once country of residence and transactional geography are included (benchmark AUC change below 0.001) and because it may act as a proxy for ethnic origin; the Bank does not take decisions that would lead to biased or discriminatory outcomes on the basis of such characteristics.

sections.text: The domain weights of 30% (customer), 25% (geography), 20% (products and services), 10% (delivery channel) and 15% (behaviour) were set by the expert panel of May and June 2025 with a two-round Delphi procedure, documented in EVD-16-EXP, using the SIRA 2025 and the statistical benchmark as inputs. Within the domains the factor weights are: customer – legal form 30%, industry or occupation 35%, ownership complexity 20%, relationship age 15%; geography – country of residence or incorporation 45%, countries of beneficial owners and representatives 25%, expected transaction countries 30%; products – product risk class 60%, declared cash use 20%, international payments 20%; channel – onboarding channel 70%, third-party payment initiation 30%; behaviour – productive TM alerts in 12 months 40%, MOTs in 24 months 35%, turnover deviation from expected activity 25%. The panel weighted behaviour lower than the benchmark (15% instead of 24%) because behaviour factors partly anticipate the outcome events and would otherwise make the class self-reinforcing; this judgement is recorded as EJ-CRR-01.

sections.heading: Factor scoring
sections.text: Each factor is scored from 1 to 5 using scoring tables approved by Financial Crime Compliance. Examples: country of residence scores 1 for EU/EEA countries of Country Risk Matrix class 1, 3 for class 3 and 5 for class 5; industry scores follow the industry risk list with 5 for cash-intensive and high-value-goods sectors such as car dealers and money service businesses; ownership complexity scores 5 for three or more ownership layers or nominee structures; the onboarding channel scores 1 for face-to-face, 2 for video identification and 3 for fully remote app onboarding. Behaviour factors score 1 when no productive alert or MOT exists and rise to 5 for two or more productive alerts in twelve months or an MOT in 24 months; the turnover deviation factor scores 5 when the observed twelve-month turnover exceeds three times the expected activity. The complete scoring tables with the rationale for each score are given in annex MDD-B and are stored in the versioned parameter file crr_scoring_v4.0.csv.

sections.heading: Class boundaries
sections.text: The class boundaries of 2.20 and 3.20 were calibrated on cohort 2023 so that the adverse-outcome rate increases materially between classes (Low 0.12%, Medium 0.61%, High 3.9% by score) and the resulting distribution is consistent with the SIRA expectation; alternative boundaries of 2.00/3.00 and 2.40/3.40 were rejected because they gave a High share by score of 4.1% and 1.6% respectively. The boundaries were confirmed on the out-of-time cohort 2024, where the adverse-outcome rates by class were 0.13%, 0.66% and 4.2%.

sections.heading: Distribution over classes
sections.text: Applied to the 2,801,900 customers in scope on 31 December 2024, version 4.0 results in the following distribution: Low 72.3% (2,025,800), Medium 23.6% (661,200), High 4.0% (112,100) and Unacceptable 0.1% (2,800), within the SIRA 2025 expectation of 3% to 5% High; 41% of High customers are High because of a mandatory trigger. By segment the High share is 3.3% for retail customers, 7.2% for sole proprietors, 9.1% for small and medium-sized enterprises, 14.1% for corporates and 26.1% for financial institutions and other legal entities.

sections.heading: Mandatory triggers and Unacceptable criteria
sections.text: The following mandatory triggers override the calculated score and assign at least the High class: politically exposed persons and their family members and close associates (screening codes PEP, PEP-FAM and PEP-RCA, for the customer, a beneficial owner or a representative); residence, incorporation or a beneficial owner in a high-risk third country identified by the European Commission; adverse information from FIU-Nederland or law enforcement (a transaction declared suspicious, a production order or a request for information); and confirmed adverse media on money laundering or its predicate offences. The class Unacceptable is assigned for a confirmed sanctions match, a shell bank, activities prohibited by the Customer Acceptance Policy (such as unlicensed money transfer services, crypto-asset service providers without registration or authorisation and unlicensed online gambling) and a refusal to provide CDD information. A trigger can be removed only by a CDD analyst with approval of Financial Crime Compliance when the underlying condition has ceased, for example twelve months after a PEP has left the public function.

sections.heading: Margin of conservatism
sections.text: Not applicable: MDL-16 does not produce risk parameters to which a margin of conservatism under CRM-STD-101 applies; the heading is retained in accordance with MRM-STD-021 §2.2. Uncertainty in the classification is addressed by the conservative scoring of missing data (section 4.3 of EVD-16-RDS), the mandatory triggers and the override process, and no adjustment is applied to scores or classes. Should monitoring indicate that the classes understate risk for a segment, the prescribed response is a recalibration of weights or boundaries under MRM-STD-050, not an overlay.

sections.heading: Discriminatory power and back-testing
sections.text: Performance was tested on the development, out-of-sample and out-of-time samples: the AUC of the CRR score for the composite adverse outcome is 0.786 on the development part of cohort 2023, 0.779 on the out-of-sample part and 0.781 on cohort 2024, and the adverse-outcome rate increases monotonically from Low to High in all three samples. The incidence of each outcome in cohort 2024 increases monotonically from Low to High: MOTs 0.8, 4.3 and 25.9 per 1,000 customers; integrity exits 0.2, 1.0 and 9.1; FIU declarations 0.1, 0.5 and 4.8. Performance thresholds for the CRR were approved by Model Risk Management: AUC of at least 0.70 and monotonic incidence across classes for each outcome.

sections.heading: Performance per segment
sections.text: Performance was measured for each segment on cohort 2024: the AUC is 0.792 (retail), 0.744 (sole proprietors), 0.763 (SMEs), 0.731 (corporates) and 0.702 (financial institutions and other legal entities), and incidence is monotonic in all segments except sole proprietors, where the MOT incidence of Low (1.3 per 1,000) slightly exceeds that of Medium (1.2). sections.heading: Benchmarking
sections.text: The CRR score is compared with a benchmark logistic regression of the composite adverse outcome on the 18 factor scores, estimated on the development part of cohort 2023: the benchmark reaches an AUC of 0.806 on cohort 2024 against 0.781 for the CRR score. The difference of 0.025 is explained mainly by the higher weight the regression assigns to the behaviour domain; the expert weighting is retained because it avoids the self-reinforcement described in section 4.3 and gives more weight to legislative risk factors with few observed outcomes, and the class agreement between the CRR and a benchmark-based classification with the same class shares is 88%.

sections.heading: Sensitivity analysis
sections.text: Sensitivity analyses cover the key assumptions, parameters and inputs: domain weights varied by ±5 percentage points (High share between 3.6% and 4.5%, AUC between 0.774 and 0.789), the benchmark weights (High share 4.4%, AUC 0.797), boundaries shifted by ±0.2, the conservative scoring of missing data (without it the High share falls by 0.2 points) and the removal of nationality (AUC change below 0.001). The results show that the class distribution is most sensitive to the weight of the behaviour domain and to the upper class boundary, which are therefore reviewed annually.

sections.heading: Stability
sections.text: The PSI of the CRR score between cohort 2023 and cohort 2024 is 0.03 and that of the class distribution 0.01. Between the two cohorts 6.2% of customers changed class, of which 71% because of a change in behaviour or product factors and 29% because of CDD updates. Stability over time is monitored semi-annually with the PSI of the score and of each factor (chapter 10).

sections.heading: Material assumptions
sections.text: The material assumptions were identified and assessed for plausibility: (A1) the composite adverse outcome is a reasonable indicator of integrity risk, although it reflects only detected cases; (A2) the legislative risk factors are relevant even where few outcomes are observed; (A3) CDD information is sufficiently current, supported by the review timeliness of 97% or more per class; and (A4) the relationship between factors and outcomes is stable over at least one year, supported by the out-of-time results. Assumption A1 implies that the back-testing cannot measure undetected risk; the model therefore relies on the expert assessment of legislative risk factors in addition to outcome data.

sections.heading: Human intervention, explanation and overrides
sections.text: Every assignment of the class High or Unacceptable, every trigger removal and every decrease of the class of a High customer is confirmed by a CDD analyst before it takes effect, and exits are decided by the Customer Integrity Committee; changes between Low and Medium take effect automatically and are reviewed in a monthly sample of 5% by CDD quality assurance. Because the class determines the extent of due diligence, the Bank treats class assignments as automated decisions within the meaning of Art. 22 GDPR, also where an analyst formally confirms them, and relies on Art. 22(2)(b) GDPR, as the classification is required by the Wwft and the AMLR. Customers can request an explanation of their class and contest it through the complaints procedure, in which a CDD analyst with authority to change the class reviews the customer's view; no explanation is given where the class results from a report to FIU-Nederland or information from FIU-Nederland, because of the prohibition of disclosure. The privacy statement informs customers that they are classified into risk classes on the basis of their due diligence data and transactions, explains the main factors and states the consequences for due diligence and review frequency. Manual overrides of the model-assigned class by CDD analysts must be justified with a reason code and evidence and approved by a senior CDD officer who is independent of the relationship manager, and their frequency and direction are monitored.

sections.heading: Monitoring plan and KPIs
sections.text: The monitoring plan, approved by the model owner on 10 February 2026 before go-live and reviewed by Model Validation – Financial Crime, defines for each KPI its calculation, amber and red thresholds, frequency, data and reference period, segments, responsible person and escalation, and it is reviewed at least annually and whenever the model changes. The KPIs are: (a) AUC of the score for the composite adverse outcome (amber below 0.72, red below 0.70); (b) monotonic incidence per outcome and class; (c) PSI of the score and of each factor against the development cohort (amber 0.10–0.25, red above 0.25); (d) High share against the SIRA expectation (amber outside 3%–5%, red outside 2%–6%); (e) share of customers with a missing or outdated class (amber above 0.5%, red above 1%); (f) override rates by segment and direction; (g) timeliness of periodic reviews per class. KPIs are computed for the whole model and for each segment and class, and override rates are assessed against the thresholds of MRM-STD-023 §6.2 and the 5% segment trigger of FEC-STD-600 §9.5. A red outcome triggers a review by the model owner and notification of Model Risk Management and Model Validation.

sections.heading: Frequency, reporting and escalation
sections.text: As a Tier 2 model MDL-16 is monitored semi-annually, with the annual report including the back-testing of FEC-STD-600 §9.4, and results are reported within 60 calendar days after the end of the reference period. Each amber result is analysed by the model owner and its cause documented; a red result, or amber on the same KPI in two consecutive cycles, is notified to Model Risk Management and Model Validation within ten business days, followed within 60 calendar days by a root cause analysis and an action plan proposing no action with justification, an overlay, recalibration, redevelopment or restriction of use. The monitoring report shows each KPI with value, threshold, traffic light and trend over the last four cycles, and presents overrides by direction, reason, magnitude and approving unit with the subsequent adverse-outcome rate of overridden and non-overridden customers. Monitoring code (repository fec-analytics/crr-monitoring) and data snapshots are version controlled so that the results are reproducible.

documents.title: CRR expert panel minutes – risk-factor weighting

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: These minutes record the expert panel that set the domain weights, factor weights, scoring tables and class boundaries of CRR version 4.0 in two sessions on 21 May 2025 and 4 June 2025, and the challenge of the outcome by Financial Crime Compliance. The panel elicited the expert judgements EJ-CRR-01 (domain weights), EJ-CRR-02 (factor weights) and EJ-CRR-03 (class boundaries) of the expert judgement log EJL-MDL16, which are justified in chapter 4 and section 5.1 of the MDD. The panel elicited the expert judgements EJ-CRR-01 (domain weights), EJ-CRR-02 (factor weights) and EJ-CRR-03 (class boundaries) of the expert judgement log EJL-MDL16, which are justified in chapter 4 and section 5.1 of the MDD.

sections.heading: Panel composition and independence
sections.text: The panel consisted of seven members: two representatives of Financial Crime Compliance (the SIRA owner and the policy lead for CDD), two senior CDD analysts of CDD Operations (retail and business), the team lead of the FIU Reporting team, the head of KYC Business Banking and, as non-voting facilitator, the lead developer of the CRR Modelling team. The members were selected for their experience with the SIRA, the Bank's customer base and investigation outcomes; together they had 94 years of experience in financial crime roles. The model owner chaired the sessions without voting on the weights. No panel member was involved in the development of the statistical benchmark, to avoid anchoring on its coefficients before the first round.

sections.heading: Elicitation method
sections.text: The weights were elicited with a two-round modified Delphi procedure: in round 1 each voting member individually and independently assigned weights to the five domains and to the factors within each domain, with a written rationale; in round 2 the members received the anonymised distribution of round 1, the SIRA 2025 ranking and the statistical benchmark results and could revise their weights. The panel result is the median of the individual round 2 weights, rounded to five percentage points and normalised to 100%; convergence was defined as an interquartile range of at most five percentage points per domain weight. Factor scoring tables were proposed by the CRR Modelling team on the basis of the adverse-outcome rates per factor value in cohort 2023 and discussed factor by factor; changes were agreed by majority, with dissent recorded.

sections.heading: Inputs to the panel
sections.text: The panel received the SIRA 2025 with the ranking of inherent risks per risk factor category, the legislative risk factors of Annexes I to III of Directive (EU) 2015/849 and the AMLR, the univariate adverse-outcome rates per factor from RDS-CRR-2025.1 (cohort 2023) and the weights implied by the benchmark regression. The benchmark implied weights of 27% (customer), 22% (geography), 19% (products and services), 8% (channel) and 24% (behaviour). The panel was informed that behaviour factors are partly correlated with the outcome definition.

sections.heading: Round 1 results
sections.text: In round 1 the medians were 30% (customer), 25% (geography), 20% (products and services), 10% (channel) and 15% (behaviour), with interquartile ranges of 5, 5, 5, 5 and 10 percentage points; behaviour did not converge, with individual weights between 10% and 25%. The individual weights of each member per domain and the written rationales are recorded in annex EXP-A; for example the FIU Reporting team lead proposed 25% for behaviour, citing the predictive value of prior MOTs, while both Financial Crime Compliance members proposed 10%, citing the risk of self-reinforcement.

deficiencies.rationale: The MDD states that politically exposed persons and their family members and close associates (screening codes PEP, PEP-FAM and PEP-RCA) trigger at least the High class. The production trigger logic maps only the code PEP; Model Validation's recalculation shows 3,410 customers with only a PEP-FAM or PEP-RCA code, of whom 2,140 are classified Low or Medium. The implementation test data contained no such customers, so the gap was not detected in implementation testing.

mitigation.text: Map PEP-FAM and PEP-RCA to the PEP trigger in the CRR engine as an emergency change, reclassify the affected customers, perform enhanced due diligence on the 2,140 customers concerned and add test cases for all screening codes.

deficiencies.rationale: The annual back-testing shows monotonic incidence at portfolio level, but for sole proprietors the MOT incidence of the Low class exceeds that of the Medium class for the second consecutive year. The deviation is analysed, but it has not yet been addressed: the proposed review of the industry risk list has no owner, scope or deadline.

mitigation.text: Complete the review of the industry risk list for cash-intensive sole proprietors with an owner and deadline, and demonstrate monotonic incidence for sole proprietors in the next back-test or document a risk-based justification.

deficiencies.rationale: In 2026, 5.6% of SME customers were overridden, above the 5% trigger, but the required methodology review has not started and is only planned for the third quarter of 2027.

mitigation.text: Start the methodology review of the SME product and source-of-funds factors, with terms of reference approved by the model owner and Financial Crime Compliance, and report the outcome in the next semi-annual monitoring report.

deficiencies.rationale: The expert judgements on domain weights, factor weights and class boundaries have a review date at the annual model review, but no conditions under which they expire, for example a sustained non-monotonic back-test or a SIRA change in the ranking of risk factor categories.

mitigation.text: Add expiry conditions to EJ-CRR-01 to EJ-CRR-03 in the expert judgement log and link them to the monitoring KPIs.

deficiencies.rationale: Implementation testing did not cover all trigger inputs: the test data set contained no customers with the PEP-FAM or PEP-RCA screening codes, and no synthetic test cases were added for them.

mitigation.text: Extend the regression test set with synthetic cases for every screening code and every trigger, and rerun implementation testing for the trigger module.

Back-test on 2026 outcomes: incidence of MOTs, integrity exits and FIU declarations monotonic from Low to High at portfolio level and in four of five segments; not monotonic for sole proprietors (MOT incidence Low 1.4 versus Medium 1.2 per 1,000).

Override analysis 2026: overall override rate 4.1% of reviewed assignments; SME segment 14.3% (amber) with 5.6% of SME customers overridden, above the FEC-STD-600 §9.5 trigger; methodology review not yet started.
Validation's independent logistic benchmark on 2026 outcomes: AUC 0.801 versus 0.778 for the CRR score; divergence explained by the documented lower behaviour weight; class agreement 87%.
